articles.headline: Texas Suburb Demands $2.3 Million for Flock Records
articles.deck: North Richland Hills cited 14 years of labor to search records as backlash grows over police license-plate tracking.

pullquote.text: give agencies a public-facing way to publish information about their [ALPR] programs, including policies, usage, and access rules to help communities better understand how the technology is being used.

body: Officials in North Richland Hills asked for $2.3 million to fulfill a public records request for documents on police use of Flock automated license plate readers. The Fort Worth suburb said searching about a terabyte of communications on errors, misuse and effectiveness would require approximately 14 years of labor at $15 per hour. The high fee request arrives as bipartisan backlash grows over AI-enabled cameras that track every vehicle that passes them.

The request was filed by Phil Mynona on behalf of the Texas Privacy Coalition and reported by the Texas Tribune. Mynona has sought similar records from more than 200 law enforcement agencies across the US. He said fees were impossible to predict. Some cities provided more than 400,000 pages of documents for free, while others charged $5,000. A Houston news station called KPRC was quoted up to $121,000 for Flock records.

Advocates say high fees obscure records that have triggered audits, arrests and decisions to remove cameras. Many officers have been found using the cameras to stalk strangers and people in their personal lives. In Texas, former officer Zachary Anthony Klein pled guilty to 100 felony counts of misuse of official information after a USA Today request helped expose Flock abuse. Governor Greg Abbott halted Flock funding and stopped issuing permits. In Oklahoma, federal judge Sara Hill ruled a search of the Flock database was unconstitutional and called the network indiscriminate mass surveillance that should require a warrant.

Flock maintains its license plate readers are designed for public safety. Courts agreed officers can access Flock databases without infringing Fourth Amendment rights. In Texas, hundreds of agencies use Flock cameras, but only 59 use transparency portals and 16 share data with the public. Audits show more than a hundred thousand warrantless searches of the Flock system every month.

art.caption: A police SUV sits beside a pole-mounted license-plate camera on a suburban Texas street at dusk. Cities across Texas use the Flock systems to scan passing vehicles, records at the center of the $2.3 million fee dispute.

articles.headline: OpenAI watermarks ChatGPT text in European Union
articles.deck: The invisible mark covers Codex and meets AI Act transparency rules that took effect August 2.
body: OpenAI will add an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union. The measure complies with the transparency rules of the EU AI Act. The rollout covers eligible users on all plans.

The watermark will roll out over the coming weeks. It applies only in the EU. Developers using the API anywhere in the world can turn it on for select models starting today. The setting is off by default. OpenAI is not making text watermarking a global default at launch.

The watermark is not a symbol. It shapes word choices in small steps. The pattern is invisible to readers. A detector can identify it. The signal travels with the text during copy and paste. OpenAI said the watermark does not identify the user. The company saw no meaningful change in performance with the watermark switched on.

OpenAI published a technical report on the method. The method is called textGrain. Researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale co-wrote the report. It describes use of a secret key to sort next-word predictions. Hundreds of small nudges accumulate in a passage. The detector needs only the text and the key to spot the signal.

Tests show editing can weaken detection. Replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66% in one test. Short passages are harder to detect. Math answers are harder to detect. Translated text is harder to detect. OpenAI said detector access will initially go only to approved researchers and expert organizations. Those groups can help evaluate reliability and responsible uses. The company cautioned that a missing watermark does not establish human authorship. The text could be too short. The text could be heavily edited. The text could come from another system.

The announcement follows a similar move by Anthropic two months earlier. Anthropic said it would watermark text generated by Claude. Anthropic is applying the measure worldwide. Some Claude users objected to the change. OpenAI had built a text watermark before. It held off on release. The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024 that the pause reflected concern about users moving to rivals without watermarking. Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI have committed to follow the EU code of practice on AI-generated content. The code covers identification of machine output. The EU requirement calls for marks that other systems can identify. The transparency rules took effect on August 2. Detector access remains limited pending further evaluation. Further testing will define practical limits.

articles.headline: Judge dismisses publisher antitrust suits against Google
articles.deck: Mehta rules that expectation of traffic does not create an antitrust duty over AI Overviews.

pullquote.text: But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.

body: US District Judge Amit Mehta has dismissed antitrust lawsuits filed by Chegg and Penske Media against Google. The publishers accused Google AI Overviews of scraping content and diverting search traffic. Mehta ruled the conduct was unfair in effect but not illegal under antitrust law.

Chegg, an education and learning platform, said Google scraped its educational content to train Gemini models and recreate answers. Penske, owner of Rolling Stone and Variety, said sites indexed for organic search had content harvested for AI answers with no way to opt out. Both suits were filed in 2025. Google sought dismissal earlier this year.

Mehta found no formal agreement requiring Google to send traffic in exchange for indexing content. He wrote that publishers had pleaded only expectation, not contract. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.” Without a formal arrangement, he held, antitrust law does not apply. Mehta previously found Google violated the law in the long running search case brought by the DOJ. The government did not obtain the harsh penalties it sought in that case.

Mehta said he did not treat the alleged harms lightly and described consequences for journalists, educators and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation. He wrote that antitrust law cannot substitute for legislative action. “The court is bound to apply the law only as it is written, not how the court or any party believes it ought to be.” The European Commission is considering the same questions. The UK has ordered Google to provide an AI opt out for sites that remain in organic search. Google is exploring direct payment for AI answers. Publishers report the pilot is not going well. Further challenges will face the same legal standard.

articles.headline: Utah lets AI prescribe acne treatment
articles.deck: The pilot covers residents 18 or older with mild-to-moderate acne and loosens physician review after early cases.
body: Utah has cleared Nolla Health to offer AI-generated prescriptions for acne treatment through a face-scanning app. The pilot allows the system to analyze acne severity and write prescriptions directly. The service is limited to Utah residents who are 18 years of age or older and have mild-to-moderate acne. The program costs $4.99 per month.

Two physicians will approve each AI-generated prescription before issue for the first 100 patients. For up to 500 patients, physicians will review prescriptions after issue. After that stage, physicians will review a sample of at least 10% of prescriptions each month and every case involving escalation or side effect. Nolla Health will direct users to a physician when the system cannot select a treatment with confidence. The company says it is the first in the country to issue initial prescriptions rather than renewals.

Several other healthcare companies are experimenting with AI-generated prescriptions in Utah. The state started allowing AI systems to renew certain medications earlier this year. The system can currently prescribe eight different skin treatments. The company says the pilot is designed to complement physicians by handling routine low-acuity cases and freeing dermatologists to focus on complex high-risk patients. Users scan their faces in the app for analysis of acne severity. The pilot uses gradually loosening physician oversight. The healthcare startup announced the service on Monday for users in the state. The camera now does part of the intake work.

articles.headline: Right Hemisphere Ages Faster Than Left Brain Map Shows
articles.deck: Local brain-age model trained on 14,748 healthy scans shows larger gaps in Alzheimer disease and mild impairment.

pullquote.text: The main message is that the brain does not appear to age uniformly,
pullquote.attr: Andrei Irimia, USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology

body: A new artificial intelligence model maps biological aging across the human brain voxel by voxel and finds the right hemisphere looks older than the left. The PNAS study trained on 14,748 healthy adult MRI scans and tested on 1,985 adults with normal cognition, mild impairment and Alzheimer disease. Gaps widen in impairment especially in frontal and temporal regions.

The model learned from MRI scans of 14,748 cognitively healthy adults from 19 to 100 years old drawn from multiple imaging cohorts. Researchers then applied it to 1,985 participants from the Alzheimer Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. That test set included 1,102 adults with normal cognition, 354 with mild cognitive impairment and 529 with Alzheimer disease. In healthy adults the estimates missed chronological age by about 5.9 years on average.

In cognitively healthy adults frontal and temporal lobes looked biologically older than occipital visual centers at the back of the brain. The deep grooves of the cortex looked older than the ridges. The gap between estimated age and true age averaged 0.40 years higher in sulci than in gyri. The right hemisphere looked older than the left. The asymmetry remained after retraining on a sample balanced between left and right handed people.

In Alzheimer disease specific subcortical structures showed markedly larger gaps than in healthy adults. The pallidum and putamen which help regulate movement and some learning showed gaps about 3.5 to 3.6 years larger. The hippocampus important for forming new memories looked more than three years older on average. People with cognitive impairment showed substantially more widespread advanced aging particularly in frontal and temporal regions. Cooler map colors mark younger looking tissue and warmer colors mark older looking tissue.

The work moves from a single global brain age score to a spatial map of local age. A single number can hide regional differences and early localized damage. The frontal lobe handles complex decision making and the hippocampus handles memory and they age at different rates. The new output maps directly back onto anatomy and is intended as a bridge between prediction and biology. It doesn’t use a single number but maps structural differences locally.

Older local age tracked worse performance on testing. In Alzheimer disease older age in regions including the right pallidum correlated with lower scores on general cognitive screening and on a measure of everyday functioning. The left right difference has no established explanation and handedness in training data did not account for it. The brain does not age uniformly within a person. The research was led by Nikhil N. Chaudhari with Andrei Irimia and colleagues. Magnetic resonance imaging uses strong magnetic fields to image internal structures. An older looking brain is often a risk factor for decline. Pattern holds in this map still.

art.caption: An older adult lies in an MRI scanner bore while a technologist monitors from the console. Researchers used such scans to build voxel-level maps of brain aging.

articles.headline: Fluent Models Fail Grounded Colombian Law Answers
articles.deck: A 1,042-item benchmark finds multiple-choice accuracy reaches 0.905 while free-text correctness never exceeds 0.45.
body: Fifteen contemporary models answer Colombian law questions with fluency but without reliability. An expert-validated benchmark of 1,042 items reports multiple-choice accuracy as high as 0.905 and free-text factual correctness no higher than 0.45 on a zero to one scale. The gap separates recognition of legal answers from production of grounded legal answers.

The benchmark spans ten areas of law and three question formats. The formats are closed multiple-choice, semi-open, and open-ended IRAC. Construction used a human-in-the-loop pipeline with multi-stage expert review. Evaluation used format-appropriate metrics across fifteen proprietary and open-weight models. Accuracy on closed questions ranged from 0.577 to 0.905 for Gemini 3.1 Pro.

Answer relevancy and factual correctness diverge. Their rank correlation is negative, with Spearman rho equal to minus 0.46. Models reliably sound responsive while frequently being wrong. The pattern carries particular concern for non-expert users. Closed-question accuracy and free-text correctness are strongly rank-correlated at rho equal to 0.94. Cheap multiple-choice screening predicts model ranking but overstates absolute reliability.

The free-text ranking holds under independent checks. An independent rubric-based LLM judge and blind human expert scoring both reproduce the free-text ranking at rho equal to 0.88. The judge examined the legal norms cited in model answers. Only about half of the norms models cite are correct. The rest are wrong or non-existent. The result points to citation as a central failure point. A fluent answer can list norms that are wrong about the law. It can also list norms that do not exist. Measurement therefore requires inspection of sources, not only inspection of conclusions.

Reliability also varies by subject and difficulty. Performance differs systematically by legal area. It follows an inverted-U across question complexity. Scores rise then fall as complexity increases. The pattern suggests limits at both ends of the scale. The middle range produces stronger results than the extremes. Area and complexity together shape the error rate. A single aggregate score therefore hides the distribution of failure. Ranking alone does not describe where models fail. Details matter in practice.

The authors state that current models require expert supervision for Colombian legal tasks. They describe grounding answers in authoritative sources as a promising path to higher reliability. They release the benchmark construction pipeline to support reproducible evaluation. The pipeline allows repeated testing with format-appropriate metrics. It also allows comparison across proprietary and open-weight systems. Multiple-choice tests remain useful for ranking. They do not certify an answer for use. The file remains open. A correct citation matters more than a confident tone. The test is the norm, not the narrative.

articles.headline: Workers prompt AI to push back
articles.deck: Interviews with 45 knowledge workers link deliberate friction to stronger ideas and less cognitive offloading.
body: Knowledge workers who ask generative AI to argue produce better solutions and think harder. Interviews with 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university point to deliberate disagreement as a check on cognitive offloading. The workers used generative AI in core tasks involving new ideas, complex problems and novel solutions. Researchers reviewed prompts and outputs from iterative chats. Friction improved performance.

One marketing professional asked AI to invent customers who would dislike an accounting certificate program under development. The contrary personas surfaced preferences for cases drawn from different industries, not one industry. One attorney asked AI to locate obscure loopholes and map how companies could exploit them. The exercise exposed realistic patterns of hard to detect misconduct by employees. One supply chain scientist adapted programs from signal processing and wireless communication suggested by AI to build a stronger program.

Expertise mattered when outputs turned strange. The supply chain scientist relied on knowledge of supply network modeling to apply unfamiliar programs. A research scholar sought papers that applied a familiar concept in contrasting settings and saw it from new angles. A lawyer requested different types of illustrative cases to test citations and wrote a stronger brief. The practical method is direct. Workers write prompts that challenge rather than agree, then judge results against knowledge, experience and professional ethics. Friction feels like opposition. It functions as assistance. Leaders can schedule shared sessions, boot camps and sandboxes where staff test tools in private environments. Discomfort is the feature, not the fault. Opposition improves the draft.

articles.headline: Renaming Tools Shifts Agent Security Scores
articles.deck: Tests on three benchmarks show wording changes move success rates without changing tasks or policies.
body: Renaming tools changes reported attack success without changing tasks, actions, policies, or scoring. On Agent Security Bench, replacing threat-related tool names with neutral names raises committed attack success by 11.67 percentage points on GPT-5-mini and by 13.21 points on Claude Haiku 4.5. The shift measures wording, not robustness.

The effect reverses on MCPTox. Replacing the original neutral tool name with an explicit threat-related name lowers attack success by 11.00 percentage points on GPT-5-mini and by 4.11 points on Claude Haiku 4.5. The underlying task, harmful action, ground truth, environment, and evaluation criteria stay fixed. Only the agent-visible representation changes.

The authors call the measure threat-preserving representation sensitivity. It records how much attack success changes when representation changes and all else holds constant. On AgentDojo, adding threat-related wording to the attack-relevant tool changes attack success by only 0.50 percentage points on GPT-4o-mini, yet benign utility falls by 5.36 points on tasks requiring that tool. A neutral name matched on token count, length, and casing reproduces 8.54 of 11.00 points of the MCPTox shift on GPT-5-mini.

A security score measured under one representation may fail to generalize across threat-preserving representations of the same security problem. The paper argues robustness claims should rest on performance across a controlled set of such representations rather than a single representation-dependent score. That means current leaderboards compare naming choices as much as model defenses. The task does not change. The policy does not change. The scoring does not change. The name on the tool changes, and the number moves. Benchmarks will need to control for that variance before the scores describe security. The test harness records the same harmful action. The difference sits in the label the agent reads. Labels leak.

articles.headline: Frontier models overstate puzzle placement confidence
articles.deck: Separate belief measure beats raw token confidence, yet models rarely ask for help.
body: Three frontier vision-language models place puzzle pieces from human instructions with 0.97 mean confidence and severe miscalibration. The study tests GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and GPT-5.5 as AI Workers directed by a human Helper. Raw action-token probabilities show ECE 0.44. A separately elicited belief distribution over candidate pieces calibrates better at ECE 0.15 and discriminates correct from incorrect placements with AUROC 0.65. The models ask for clarification on only 3.5-16.7 percent of turns.

Elicited uncertainty rises predictably with instruction vagueness. It does not rise with competing referents in context, even when those increase errors. Human Helpers receive the default Worker message in a controlled study with N equal to 210 participants. They accept 78 percent of wrong placements. They cannot tell right from wrong, with AUC 0.50. Precise descriptions and well-targeted hedges cut wrong-move acceptance to 36 percent while largely preserving correct-move acceptance.

The result compensates for missing shared awareness such as not seeing the Worker action. The Helper must recognize uncertainty and act on it. The Worker must identify and communicate its uncertainty over which candidate object a description refers to. That exchange becomes fragile when descriptions are ambiguous, similar referents compete, or partners see different things. A deployable hedge derived from the model own belief entropy inherits that signal weakness and can do more harm than good. Externalized uncertainty helps a human partner only when it is accurately targeted. The task requires partners to establish references through interaction and hold steady when each reference is clear for now. Silence remains the default.

boxes.title: Three Records Fights
paras: Three places show how license plate readers are being challenged. In North Richland Hills, city officials asked one group to pay $2.3 million before it would fulfill a public records request for Flock data. In Florida, crowdsourced mapping projects currently show nearly 10,000 cameras, with concentrations around major metropolitan areas. In Marin County, MCSO was reported to have shared automated license plate reader data from its Flock Safety system with out-of-state and federal agencies. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California sent a demand letter and request for records under the California Public Records Act. The Texas Tribune reported the North Richland Hills request on Monday. This is likely an undercounting. Each case turns on access to records about how police departments use systems that track every vehicle that passes them.

boxes.title: The Useful Opponent
paras: Disagreement works better than agreement when using AI for work. Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity and problem solving. People who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low quality solutions. Scholars refer to the problem as cognitive offloading. A pilot used ChatGPT as a thinking partner in an undergraduate research methods and statistics course during Spring 2025 with N = 14. It combined measures of statistical learning, AI literacy and critical thinking with instructor field notes and student artifacts. Prompting a model to fight a point of view can raise novel solutions.
